title: SR&ED Work Performed Outside Canada Rules | FAQ
description: Can you claim SR&ED work performed by employees outside of Canada? Read our FAQ on foreign R&D limits and the 10% permissible salary cap.
summary: SR&ED work must generally be carried out in Canada, but Canadian claimants may include salary or wages for SR&ED performed outside Canada by Canadian-resident employees when the work is integral to, and solely supports, SR&ED in Canada and is not taxed abroad. The claim is capped at 10% of total SR&ED salary or wages in Canada.

The claim is capped at 10% of total SR&ED salary or wages in Canada.

Canada’s research and development (R&D) tax incentive architecture—anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program and complemented by ten distinct provincial and territorial tax credit regimes—has undergone its most significant legislative transformation in over a decade. Enacted through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, the federal reforms apply retroactively to taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (and to depreciable capital property acquired or lease costs first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024). These statutory amendments double the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% federal Investment Tax Credit (ITC) from $3 million to $6 million, widen the prior-year taxable capital phase-out corridor from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million, extend the 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a three-year average consolidated revenue phase-out, and restore both immediate income deductibility under paragraph 37(1)(b) and ITC eligibility under subsection 127(9) for SR&ED capital expenditures and Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE). Earlier legislative action under Bill C-69 (Royal Assent on June 20, 2024, retroactive to January 1, 2020) also amended subsection 127(9) to exclude bona fide public-authority loans with reasonable repayment terms ("excluded loans" under subsection 12(11)) from the definition of government assistance, reversing the adverse expenditure-pool grind crystallized in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178).

Concurrently, the sub-national landscape has diverged into aligned jurisdictions, independent structural reformers, and holdouts. In Québec, the 2025–2026 Budget abolished seven legacy R&D tax measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified, fully refundable Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (Crédit d'impôt pour la recherche, l'innovation et la commercialisation, or CRIC), which provides a 30% credit on the first $1 million of qualified expenditures above an employee-linked exclusion threshold (and 20% on the excess) while expanding coverage to capital equipment and pre-commercialization activities such as regulatory validation and product design. British Columbia expressly harmonized its provincial regime with the federal Bill C-15 reforms via B.C. Budget 2026 (announced February 17, 2026), adopting the $6 million expenditure limit, the $15 million–$75 million capital phase-out, ECPC refundability, capital expenditure restoration, and permanent statutory status for its 10% SR&ED credit. Conversely, Saskatchewan implemented a province-specific expansion doubling its CCPC refundable expenditure ceiling from $1 million to $2 million, while Ontario (8% refundable OITC capped at $3 million; 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC; 20% refundable OBRITC) and Alberta (8% base and 20% incremental Innovation Employment Grant capped at $4 million on current expenditures only) retained their independent caps and expenditure bases.
1. Federal Statutory Architecture and Legislative Evolution
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Structure of the Federal SR&ED Program

The federal SR&ED Program is not a discretionary grant scheme; it is a statutory entitlement codified within the Income Tax Act (the Act) and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (the Regulations), jointly overseen by the Department of Finance Canada (which formulates tax policy and legislative text) and administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (which conducts technical and financial compliance reviews), with small businesses submitting on average 64% to 65% of all annual SR&ED claims. The statutory mechanism delivers tax relief through two distinct, sequential stages:

items: Immediate Income Deduction and Indefinite Pool Carryforward (Section 37): Under subsection 37(1) of the Act, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada in a taxation year may accumulate allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred in Canada in a running cumulative account known as the pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures. The taxpayer may deduct any portion or all of the positive pool balance in computing income from the business for the current taxation year, or carry the undeducted balance forward indefinitely to offset business income in any future taxation year.

Investment Tax Credits and Cash Refundability (Sections 127 and 127.1): Under subsections 127(5), 127(9), and 127(10.1) of the Act, a taxpayer earns an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) calculated as a percentage (15% basic rate or 35% enhanced rate) of the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool at the end of the taxation year. Unused non-refundable ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years or carried forward up to 20 taxation years to reduce federal Part I tax otherwise payable. Under section 127.1 and subsection 127.1(2.01), eligible claimants—most notably Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) and, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs)—may receive up to 100% of their unused enhanced ITCs on current expenditures (and 40% on capital expenditures) as an immediate cash refund.

body.text: Crucially, the Section 37 deduction and the Section 127 ITC interact across consecutive taxation years to prevent a double tax benefit on the same dollar of expenditure. Specifically, under paragraph 37(1)(e) of the Act, any federal SR&ED ITC deducted against Part I tax under subsection 127(5) or refunded in cash under section 127.1 in a preceding taxation year reduces the taxpayer's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the immediately following taxation year. If the reduction under paragraph 37(1)(e) (combined with assistance reductions under paragraph 37(1)(d)) causes the Section 37 pool balance to become negative at year-end, the negative balance is brought into the taxpayer's taxable income under paragraph 12(1)(v) (or paragraph 12(1)(t) where applicable), and an equivalent amount is added back to the pool in the subsequent year under paragraph 37(1)(c.1) to reset the pool to nil.
1.2 Statutory Definition of SR&ED Under Subsection 248(1)

Historically located in subsection 2900(1) of the Income Tax Regulations, the legal definition of "scientific research and experimental development" was migrated into subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act so that substantive changes to the scope of eligible R&D require an Act of Parliament rather than an Order in Council. Under subsection 248(1), "scientific research and experimental development" means a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four qualifying pillars:

items: Paragraph (a) — Basic Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, traditionally performed in university or government laboratories as well as within biotechnology, nanotechnology, advanced materials, and computer application businesses.
Paragraph (b) — Applied Research: Work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.

Paragraph (c) — Experimental Development: Work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products or processes, including incremental improvements thereto.

Paragraph (d) — Support Work: Work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of work described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

body.text: Statutory Exclusions: Paragraphs 248(1)(e) through (k)

Subsection 248(1) explicitly carves out seven categories of commercial, routine, or non-technological activity, collectively termed excluded work, which do not qualify as SR&ED even if performed by qualified scientists or engineers. Specifically, excluded work comprises market research or sales promotion under paragraph (e); quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products or processes under paragraph (f); research in the social sciences or the humanities under paragraph (g); prospecting, exploring or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum or natural gas under paragraph (h); the commercial production of a new or improved material, device or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process under paragraph (i); style changes (such as iterating a product's aesthetic form, finish, or proportions without resolving an underlying technological uncertainty) under paragraph (j); and routine data collection under paragraph (k).

As the CRA's Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives emphasize, the primary distinction between eligible support work under paragraph (d) (such as data collection or testing) and excluded work under paragraphs (f) or (k) (routine testing or routine data collection) is purpose and proportionality. If data collection or testing is carried out specifically for the purpose of testing a hypothesis to resolve a scientific or technological uncertainty—and its scope, duration, and scale are commensurate with the needs of that investigation—it qualifies under paragraph 248(1)(d). Conversely, activities related to acquiring knowledge or know-how that already exists—such as employee training, on-the-job learning, hiring experts or consultants to apply what they already know, or purchasing proprietary knowledge—do not meet the requirement of attempting to achieve scientific or technological advancement and cannot be claimed.
1.3 Comprehensive Breakdown of the 2024–2026 Federal Legislative Reforms

Between June 2024 and March 2026, Parliament enacted two landmark statutes—Bill C-69 and Bill C-15—that overhauled the financial parameters and expenditure eligibility rules of the SR&ED Program. While the 2024 Fall Economic Statement initially proposed increasing the enhanced expenditure limit to $4.5 million, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 (which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026) legislated the limit at $6 million effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

body.text: 2.2 Mathematical Determination of the Expenditure Limit
A. Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula for CCPCs (Subsection 127(10.2))

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, a CCPC (and its associated corporations, which must allocate the group limit on Schedule T2SCH49 pursuant to subsection 127(10.21)) is entitled to a base expenditure limit of $6,000,000. Under the standard taxable capital method, this $6,000,000 limit begins to decrease linearly once the combined taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated corporations in the immediately preceding taxation year reaches $15,000,000, and is reduced to nil at $75,000,000. where:

A = nil if the taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC for its immediately preceding taxation year (or, if the CCPC is associated with other corporations, the total taxable capital employed in Canada of the CCPC and all associated corporations) is $15,000,000 or less; in any other case, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that taxable capital exceeds $15,000,000.

For taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024, the maximum expenditure limit was $3,000,000, phasing out over a $40,000,000 span between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. Similarly, for defining a "qualifying corporation" for the 40% refund on the 15% basic ITC, the qualifying income limit under subsection 127.1(2) of the Act uses the formula $500,000 × [($40,000,000 − A) / $40,000,000] for taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024; its taxable capital thresholds mirror those in subsection 127(10.2), which were increased from $10 million and $50 million to $15 million and $75 million for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024.

If a corporation has a short taxation year or multiple taxation years ending in the same calendar year, the expenditure limit is reduced accordingly. Furthermore, anti-avoidance provisions deem two or more corporations to be associated with each other if one of the main reasons for their separate corporate existence is to reduce income tax otherwise payable or to increase the amount of refundable SR&ED ITCs available.
B. Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) and the 3-Year Revenue Phase-Out (Subsection 127(10.6))

To prevent domestic technology and industrial firms from losing access to the 35% refundable SR&ED credit upon becoming public corporations, Bill C-15 amended subsection 127(10.1) and subsection 127.1(2.01) to extend the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

To qualify as an ECPC throughout a taxation year under subsection 127(9), a corporation must satisfy four statutory conditions: (1) it is a public corporation listed on a designated stock exchange; (2) it is resident in Canada; (3) it is not controlled directly or indirectly in any manner whatever by one or more non-resident persons; and (4) it would not be controlled by a particular person if all shares of its capital stock owned by non-resident persons were owned by that particular person. A Canadian-resident corporation at least 90% of the issued shares of each class of whose capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more such corporations (an eligible subsidiary) also qualifies as an ECPC.

The expenditure limit for an ECPC is phased out under subsection 127(10.6) based on average annual revenue over the 3 preceding fiscal years, as reported in the consolidated financial statements of the ECPC's consolidated group (defined in subsection 127(9) as a group of entities where an ultimate parent entity is required to prepare consolidated financial statements—or would be so required if its equity interests were traded on a public securities exchange—presenting the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as those of a single economic entity). If the entity has fewer than three preceding fiscal years (that is, one or two fiscal years), the average annual revenue is calculated over the actual number of preceding fiscal years. The revenue phase-out reduces the $6,000,000 limit when average annual revenue over the previous three fiscal years exceeds $15,000,000 and reduces the limit to nil at $75,000,000 or greater:
where:

A = nil if the average annual revenue over the three fiscal years immediately preceding the taxation year (based on the ECPC's own financial statements or, for a member of a consolidated group, the consolidated financial statements of the group) is $15,000,000 or less; in any other case, A is the lesser of $60,000,000 and the amount by which that average annual revenue exceeds $15,000,000.
C. Elective Revenue Method for High-Capital, Low-Revenue CCPCs

For taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, a CCPC (or an associated group of CCPCs) may elect on a prescribed form under subsection 127(10.31) (or, for an associated group, subsection 127(10.32)) to disapply the taxable capital phase-out under subsection 127(10.2) and instead determine its $6,000,000 expenditure limit using the 3-year average annual revenue method under subsection 127(10.6). This election benefits capital-intensive CCPCs whose prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15 million due to equity or debt financings, but whose three-year average annual revenue remains below $15 million (or below $75 million). Where an associated group of CCPCs makes this election, all associated CCPCs in the group must jointly elect the revenue method; the calculation uses the total of all amounts of average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of each corporation that is a member of the group for the preceding three fiscal years (regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire three-year period), includes reasonable shares from partnerships or trusts, and permits reasonable adjustments such as eliminating intra-group sales of goods or services so that the annual revenue reflects that of a single economic entity.
2.3 Carryback, Carryforward, Loss Restriction Events, and Recapture

items: Carryback and Carryforward of Unused ITCs: To the extent that an SR&ED ITC earned in a taxation year is neither deducted against Part I tax otherwise payable under subsection 127(5) nor refunded in cash under section 127.1 (noting that any refunded ITC is deemed to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable, thereby reducing the balance available for carryover), the unused ITC may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years or carried forward up to 20 subsequent taxation years. Carrybacks are restricted to the lesser of the current year's unapplied and unrefunded ITC and the amount by which Part I tax otherwise payable in the previous taxation year exceeds the ITC available in that previous year. Note also that while repayments of government or non-government assistance or contract payments generate an ITC at the rate that would have been earned in the year the assistance or contract payment was originally received, cash refunds cannot be claimed for ITCs generated by repayments of assistance or contract payments.

Loss Restriction Events (Acquisition of Control): Upon an acquisition of control of a corporation (or when a trust gets a new majority-interest beneficiary), a deemed taxation year-end is triggered immediately prior to the acquisition, and the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures is reduced to nil under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h). Similarly, an acquisition of control restricts the carryforward of unused ITCs earned before the acquisition of control and the carryback of unused ITCs earned after the acquisition of control. The undeducted portion of the Section 37 pool prior to the loss restriction event may be reinstated and deducted in subsequent taxation years only if (1) the business to which the SR&ED expenditure related continues to be carried on for profit or with a reasonable expectation of profit, and (2) the deduction is applied only to the extent that income for the taxation year (before the SR&ED pool deduction) is derived from that same business or a similar business.

Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credits (Subsections 127(27) to (36)): If a claimant acquires a property (such as materials transformed into a commercial asset or custom product, ASA capital equipment acquired after December 15, 2024, Shared-Use-Equipment, animals/growing things used in SR&ED, or physical property acquired under an arm's-length SR&ED contract) on which an SR&ED ITC was claimed, and subsequently disposes of the property or converts it to commercial use, the claimant must add a recapture of ITC directly to its federal Part I tax payable for the year of disposition or conversion. For Shared-Use-Equipment, the recapture amount under paragraph 127(27)(d) is the lesser of the total ITC obtained for the property as first- and second-term SUE and the ITC calculated on 50% of the proceeds of disposition (or 50% of the fair market value if converted to commercial use). Under paragraph 37(1)(c.2) (and paragraph 37(1)(c.3) for partnership recapture excess), any ITC recaptured in the prior taxation year is added back to increase the claimant's Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. Where intellectual property (IP) belongs to the payer under the terms of an SR&ED contract, disposing of the IP or converting it to commercial use does not trigger ITC recapture because the IP always belonged to the payer as it was generated rather than being acquired as physical property.

body.text: 3. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies

To qualify for federal SR&ED incentives, expenditures must first be allowable SR&ED expenditures incurred for work carried on in Canada under Section 37, and then adjusted to determine qualified SR&ED expenditures under subsection 127(9) for ITC calculation on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim).
3.1 Election Between the Proxy Method and the Traditional Method

In Part 3 of Form T661 (Lines 160 and 162), a claimant must elect annually whether to compute its SR&ED expenditures using the Proxy Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)) or the Traditional Method (clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)). Once Form T661 is filed for a taxation year, the chosen method cannot be changed for that taxation year, although a claimant may switch methods from year to year. If a claimant does not elect the Proxy Method, the Traditional Method applies by default.

body.text: 3.2 Salary or Wages and Specified Employee Restrictions

Under subsection 248(1), "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the Act (Sections 5 to 8), including vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, and cash outlays for taxable benefits under section 6 (or non-cash taxable benefits if the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes GST/HST or PST where input tax credits are claimable, and the underlying costs are not claimed separately as a business expense). Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages exclude the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, pension contributions), extended vacation or extended sick leave pay, retiring allowances (which may only be considered as overhead under the Traditional Method if directly related and incremental), and stock option benefits (section 7), which were disallowed as SR&ED expenditures by legislative amendment effective after November 14, 2005, following Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2005 TCC 149).

items: Allocation of Directly Engaged Wages & the ASA (90%) Rule: Only the portion of an employee's salary or wages that can reasonably be considered to relate to hands-on SR&ED work in Canada can be included. However, under the All or Substantially All (ASA) rule (subsection 2900(5) of the Regulations), if an employee spends 90% or more of their employment time directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada, 100% of their eligible salary or wages qualifies.

Unpaid Remuneration — The 180-Day Rule (Subsection 78(4)): If accrued salary or wages allocated to SR&ED remain unpaid 180 days after the end of the taxation year in which the expense was incurred (with payment on the 180th day accepted as timely), the unpaid amount is deemed not to have been incurred in that taxation year; instead, it is deemed to be an SR&ED expenditure incurred in the taxation year in which it is actually paid. While reasonable vacation/holiday pay and deferred amounts under a statutory salary deferral arrangement (subsection 248(1)) are deemed paid within 180 days for Section 37 purposes, neither deemed-paid unpaid vacation/deferred amounts nor prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310 of Form T661) may be included in the salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount.

Permissible Salary or Wages for SR&ED Outside Canada (Subsections 37(1.4), 37(1.5), and 37(2)): While SR&ED must generally be carried on in Canada (including Canada's Exclusive Economic Zone under subsection 37(1.3)), a claimant may claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work performed outside Canada if five cumulative statutory conditions are met: (1) the SR&ED work was directly undertaken by an employee of the claimant (never a subcontractor); (2) the employee was a resident of Canada at the time the expense was incurred; (3) the work was related to a business of the claimant; (4) the work constituted an integral part of, and was solely in support of, SR&ED carried on in Canada by the claimant; and (5) the salary or wages were not subject to an income or profits tax in another country. The maximum permissible foreign salary (Line 307 for non-specified employees plus Line 309 for specified employees on Form T661) is limited to the lesser of the actual eligible foreign SR&ED wages and 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages for SR&ED carried on in Canada (Line 306 of Form T661), with specified employees restricted on Line 309 to (10% × Line 306) − Line 307.

body.text: Rules and Caps for "Specified Employees"

A specified employee is defined in subsection 248(1) as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the claimant or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly, at any time in the year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or of a related corporation. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions, and founders remunerated solely through dividends earn zero SR&ED wage expenditures and zero proxy base:

items: Complete Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration (Subsection 37(9)): Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees cannot be claimed as SR&ED salary or wages (whereas bonuses and profit-based remuneration paid to non-specified employees qualify for direct SR&ED wages, though they are excluded from the PPA salary base for all employees).

Direct SR&ED Salary Cap — 5 × YMPE: The maximum direct SR&ED salary or wages claimable for a specified employee cannot exceed 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee of the claimant (subsection 37(9.1)):Maximum SR&ED salary or wages = 5 × YMPE × (number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee ÷ 365)Associated corporations employing the same specified employee must allocate this maximum limit using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED)).

Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Salary Base Cap — Lesser of 75% of Total Wages or 2.5 × YMPE (Regulations 2900(7) to 2900(10)): When calculating the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 on which the 55% PPA is computed, the amount included for a specified employee cannot exceed the lesser of (a) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year), or (b) 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by the number of days employed in the taxation year (with no proration for the portion of the year the individual was not a specified employee):Specified employee salary base = lesser of (75% × salary or wages for the year) and (2.5 × YMPE × number of days employed in the taxation year ÷ 365)Under subsections 2900(8) and 2900(10) of the Regulations, this 2.5 × YMPE limit must be shared across associated corporations (including individuals related to the corporation and partnerships with related/associated partners).

body.text: 3.3 The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) and the Overall Cap Formula

For claimants electing the Proxy Method, the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under subsection 2900(4) of the Regulations is calculated in Part 5 of Form T661 as 55% of the salary base (Line 818, which equals Line 814 non-specified employee base plus Line 816 specified employee base):
PPA = 55% × salary base (Line 818)

To claim the full 55% PPA on Line 502, the claimant must also satisfy the Overall Cap on the PPA under subsection 2900(6) of the Regulations, which ensures that total qualified SR&ED expenditures, the PPA, and specific statutory deductions do not exceed total business expenditures deducted for tax purposes in the taxation year:
PPA ≤ A − (B + C)

In this formula, A is the total of all amounts deducted in computing net income for tax purposes from all businesses carried on by the claimant for the year (including cost of goods sold, per Schedule T2SCH1); B is the sum of deductions claimed in the year under sections 20 (e.g., Capital Cost Allowance [CCA], interest, bad debts), 24 (ceasing to carry on business), 26 (banks), 30 (improving land for farming), 32 (insurance agents/brokers), 37 (the current-year SR&ED expenditure deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1), 66 to 66.8 (exploration and development expenses), and 104 (trusts) of the Act; and C is the total of expenditure amounts incurred for the use of, or the right to use, a building (building rent). As noted in the CRA's Prescribed Proxy Amount Policy, the overall cap under Regulation 2900(6) will not restrict the 55% PPA so long as the claimant has deducted more than $55 of non-SR&ED operating expenses (excluding the deductions in B and C) for each $100 of eligible salary included in the salary base.
3.4 Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed

Under subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I)–(II), subclause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(V), and paragraph 2900(2)(a) of the Regulations, a claimant may claim the laid-down cost (invoice price, customs and excise duties, freight, storage, and preparatory service costs such as contractor galvanization—or raw materials, direct labour, and production overhead for internally manufactured inventory, even under the Proxy Method) of materials for SR&ED in the taxation year in which the materials are actually consumed or transformed, rather than the year they are acquired or placed into inventory. Where materials are purchased from a non-arm's length supplier, the ITC is restricted under subsection 127(11.6) to the actual cost to the non-arm's length entity, excluding any intercompany profit markup.

items: Physical and Tangible Requirement: Per the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, "materials for SR&ED" means physical and tangible raw materials, substances, or other items (in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a thing at a given moment in the SR&ED process—either the tangible object on which the SR&ED is being carried out or the tangible object that results from the SR&ED. Broken or used laboratory supplies (petri dishes, beakers, flasks, pipettes), cleaning supplies, used lubricants, CDs/DVDs, water, and general utilities (electricity, natural gas, or oil used to run equipment or heat a laboratory or greenhouse) do not qualify as materials for SR&ED, though they may qualify as overhead under the Traditional Method (energy qualifies as a material consumed only if it becomes an integral part of a physical/chemical conversion process or is itself the subject of SR&ED).
Materials Consumed: Materials that are destroyed, absorbed, broken down, or rendered virtually valueless as a result of the SR&ED work. Materials consumed are not subject to ITC recapture.

Materials Transformed: Materials integrated into a prototype, pilot plant, experimental production run, or commercial asset that retains value or utility after testing. While the cost of materials transformed is claimable as a current SR&ED expenditure in the year of transformation, if the resulting property is later sold or converted to commercial use, the original material cost (excluding in-house manufacturing labour and overhead) is subject to ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to (36).

body.text: 3.5 Subcontractors (80% Rule) and Third-Party Payments

A taxpayer may claim expenditures for SR&ED performed on its behalf in Canada under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01) (SR&ED contracts) or payments made to approved universities, colleges, research institutes, approved associations, granting councils, or tax-exempt non-profit R&D corporations under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii) (third-party payments).

items: 100% Section 37 Deductibility vs. 80% Section 127 ITC Inclusion: For arm's-length SR&ED contracts and third-party payments, 100% of the eligible expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool. However, under paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), only 80% of arm's-length contract expenditures and third-party payments qualify for the federal ITC (with the 20% reduction deducted on Line 529 of Form T661).

Taxable Supplier and Unpaid Amount Rules: To qualify for ITCs, an arm's-length SR&ED contract expenditure must be paid or payable to a taxable supplier for SR&ED carried on in Canada (payments to non-taxable foreign suppliers are deducted on Line 528 of Form T661 and earn no ITC). Under the unpaid amount rules, any current expenditure (other than salary or wages) not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year is deducted on Line 520 of Form T661 and is only added to qualified expenditures (at 80% for contracts) in the subsequent year when actually paid.

Non-Arm's Length (NAL) SR&ED Contracts: Where a claimant contracts SR&ED to a non-arm's length performer, the payer's contract payment is an allowable Section 37 deduction but is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures (and the payment received from the NAL payer is not treated as a contract payment reducing the performer's pool), or the NAL performer and payer may jointly file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer the performer's qualified expenditures to the payer (Line 540 of Form T661).

Distinction Between SR&ED Contracts and Third-Party Payments: Under an SR&ED contract (subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01)), the SR&ED work is controlled by the payer, the rights to the work are exclusive to the payer, the contract is usually limited to one payer with a commercial focus, and the tax treatment is accrual. Under a third-party payment (subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii)), the SR&ED work is controlled by the performer (often basic or applied research with multiple payers), the payer holds a non-exclusive preferential right to exploit the results, and the claimant must complete and attach Form T1263 (Third-Party Payments for SR&ED) for each payment.

body.text: 3.6 Cloud Computing, Software Licences, and Data Costs

Under the Act and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy and SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, software subscriptions, cloud computing infrastructure, and data licences are governed by strict classification rules:

items: Ineligibility as "Materials": Because software, data licences, and cloud computing services are not physical, tangible substances in a solid, liquid, or gaseous state that compose the body of a physical thing, they do not qualify as "materials consumed or transformed".

Treatment Under the Proxy Method: When a claimant elects the Proxy Method, overhead of every kind—including software subscriptions and general utilities/hosting—is already represented by the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4); claiming software subscriptions or cloud hosting separately under the Proxy Method would constitute claiming the expense twice and is disallowed. (Outright capital purchases of computer hardware or depreciable software acquired after December 15, 2024, that are not GPOEF and are intended to be used ASA [≥ 90%] in SR&ED in Canada are evaluated under the restored capital expenditure rules.)

Treatment Under the Traditional Method: Under the Traditional Method, a portion of an expenditure of a current nature qualifies under paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the Regulations if it satisfies two cumulative tests: (a) the Directly Related Test (having a direct linkage with no intervening step to the SR&ED work, the SR&ED staff, or the machinery/equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED), and (b) the Incremental Test (the expenditure would not have been incurred had the SR&ED prosecution not occurred). Fixed monthly telecommunications or internet subscriptions fail the incremental test because they would be incurred regardless of SR&ED, whereas separately identifiable, metered charges incurred specifically and solely for SR&ED experimentation qualify.

body.text: 3.7 Restored Capital Expenditures, Lease Costs, and Shared-Use-Equipment (Post–December 15, 2024)

Pursuant to Bill C-15 and the CRA's updated SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (June 29, 2026), SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (June 8, 2026), and SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (May 22, 2026), capital property and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024) are once again eligible for SR&ED tax incentives:

items: All or Substantially All (ASA ≥ 90%) Capital Expenditures (Paragraph 37(1)(b)): Depreciable property (new or used, such as experimental machinery, tooling, or moulds) acquired and available for use (subsections 13(27) and 37(1.2)) after December 15, 2024, qualifies for 100% inclusion in the Section 37 deductible pool and 100% inclusion in the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (reported on Line 390 and itemized on Lines 262–263 and Part 6B Box 780 of Form T661) if, at the time of acquisition, the claimant intended either (1) to use the property during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life to perform SR&ED in Canada, or (2) to consume ASA (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. For CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6 million expenditure limit, the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures is 40% refundable (an effective 14% cash refund). Because amounts deducted under paragraph 37(1)(b) are deemed by subsection 37(6) to be Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) allowed to the taxpayer, claimants must not claim duplicate CCA on Schedule T2SCH8.

Exclusions for Land, Buildings, and the Regulation 2903 Cleanroom Exception: Non-depreciable property (such as land) and buildings or leasehold interests in buildings are excluded from SR&ED capital expenditures under paragraph 37(8)(e) (though structural steel, concrete footings, foundations, stairs, and platforms attached to a building exclusively to support or provide access to machinery fall under CCA Class 8 and are not excluded as buildings, nor are non-rigid tents or air-supported fabric domes). Furthermore, third-party payments after December 15, 2024, enabling an arm's-length approved research institute/association or an approved university/college to acquire a building may be allowed under subparagraphs 37(8)(e)(iii)–(iv) if the payer acquires no interest in the building. For direct acquisitions by a claimant after December 15, 2024, the sole building exception is a prescribed special-purpose building satisfying Section 2903 of the Income Tax Regulations, which requires: (1) working areas designed and constructed to have a displacement in any direction of not more than 0.02 micrometres; and (2) an interior airspace containing, per 0.028 cubic metres of interior airspace, fewer than 350 airborne particles ≤ 0.1 µm in diameter (and zero > 0.1 µm), fewer than 75 airborne particles ≤ 0.2 µm (and zero > 0.2 µm), fewer than 30 airborne particles ≤ 0.3 µm (and zero > 0.3 µm), or fewer than 10 airborne particles ≤ 0.5 µm (and zero > 0.5 µm).

Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE — Paragraph 127(9)(a)(iii)): Depreciable property acquired and available for use after December 15, 2024, that does not meet the 90% ASA test qualifies as Shared-Use-Equipment (SUE) if it is new property (never used, acquired for use, or rented before acquisition), is not GPOEF, is not Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the Regulations (such as buildings or equipment intended to be used during commercial plant/line commissioning, though pilot plant equipment is permitted), and its actual cumulative SR&ED operating time exceeds 50% ("primarily") of its total operating time. Under the SUE rules, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowed money costs under section 21 and adjusted for non-arm's length transfers under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies for the SR&ED ITC at the end of the First Period (the end of the first taxation year occurring at least 12 months after acquisition/available-for-use), and an additional 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (for a cumulative 50% of capital cost) qualifies at the end of the Second Period (the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after acquisition/available-for-use), reported on Line 504 and Part 6C Box 788 of Form T661. SUE capital costs are not added to the Section 37 pool; instead, they are depreciated under normal CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8, with any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reducing the class UCC in the subsequent year.

Equipment Lease Costs: Current lease expenditures first becoming payable on or after December 16, 2024, for the right to use equipment (excluding buildings and, under the Proxy Method, GPOEF) qualify for SR&ED incentives if the equipment is used ASA (≥ 90%) in SR&ED (or on Line 360 under the Traditional Method if used < 90% in SR&ED and meeting the directly related and incremental tests).

body.text: 4. Interaction with Government Assistance, Grants, and Provincial Credits

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsections 127(9), 127(18), 127(19), and 127(20) of the Act, the SR&ED regime operates on a net-expenditure basis: any government assistance, non-government assistance (paragraph 12(1)(x)), or contract payment in respect of SR&ED that a claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date of the income tax return reduces both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (reported on Lines 429–432 and Lines 513–517 of Form T661). Non-arm's length parties may allocate assistance among themselves using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length). Note also that payments received from the Canadian Commercial Corporation in respect of funds received from a foreign government or public authority are a "prescribed amount" under Regulation 4606 and do not constitute a contract payment reducing SR&ED pools.
4.1 Key Rules Governing Assistance and the "Proxy Shield"

items: Project-by-Project Allocation: Per Guide T4088 and the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, assistance and contract payments are applied on a project-by-project basis. If government funding on Project 1 exceeds Project 1's eligible SR&ED expenditures, that excess reduces Project 1's pool to nil (never negative) and does not reduce the qualified expenditures of an unfunded Project 2 in the same taxation year (if Project 1 is not completed by year-end, the excess assistance carries forward to reduce Project 1's expenditures in the subsequent taxation year).

The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) Shield: When a claimant elects the Proxy Method and receives a salary-based R&D grant—such as a contribution from the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP)—the grant reduces the net qualified expenditure pool on Line 513/515 of Form T661 dollar-for-dollar, but it does NOT reduce the salary base in Part 5 of Form T661 used to calculate the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount. Moreover, under the Proxy Method, overhead-specific assistance does not reduce the Section 37 deductible pool because overhead expenditures are not included in the pool. Consequently, an employee whose $100,000 SR&ED salary is 80% funded by an $80,000 NRC IRAP grant still generates a full $55,000 PPA (55% × $100,000) in addition to the $20,000 of unsubsidized salary, leaving $75,000 of net qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the 35% federal ITC ($26,250 credit) on top of the $80,000 IRAP grant.

Bona Fide Public Authority Loans (Bill C-69 Carve-Out vs. Forgivable Grants): Following the Federal Court of Appeal decision in CAE Inc. v. The King (2022 FCA 178), where non-forgivable Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative (SADI) loans were held to be government assistance because their terms were not strictly commercial, Parliament enacted Bill C-69 (Royal Assent June 20, 2024, retroactive to January 1, 2020, for loans made after December 31, 2019). Under amended subsection 127(9) and subsection 12(11), a bona fide "excluded loan" with reasonable repayment terms from a Canadian public authority is not considered government assistance and does not reduce SR&ED expenditures (affected claimants may file amended returns for open taxation years to reverse prior loan reductions even if the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline has passed). Conversely, non-repayable grants, subsidies, and forgivable loans (where repayment is conditional solely upon future project revenues or profits without firm repayment obligations) continue to constitute government assistance.

Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credits as Government Assistance: All provincial and territorial R&D tax credits claimed (or earned and added to a carryforward pool, unless formally waived/renounced on or before the tax return filing-due date) constitute "government assistance" reported on Line 429 and Line 513 of Form T661, reducing the federal qualified expenditure pool for the same taxation year.

body.text: 4.2 Worked Financial Stacking Example (CCPC in Ontario With NRC IRAP, OITC, ORDTC, and Federal SR&ED)

To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics of the Proxy Method, the 80% contractor rule, the PPA shield on NRC IRAP grants, and the inter-credit grind with Ontario's OITC and ORDTC, consider a qualifying Ontario CCPC for its taxation year ended December 31, 2025 (beginning after December 15, 2024, with prior-year taxable capital below $15 million and prior-year taxable income below $500,000):

items: Direct SR&ED Wages (Non-Specified Employees in Ontario): $1,000,000
Materials Consumed in SR&ED: $100,000
Arm's-Length Canadian SR&ED Subcontractor: $200,000
New ASA (≥ 90%) Lab Equipment Acquired in March 2025: $300,000
NRC IRAP Wage Subsidy Grant Received: $250,000

body.text: Step-by-Step Computation of Qualified Expenditures and Tax Credits

items: Part 3 Form T661 — Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400): Summing direct wages ($1,000,000), materials consumed ($100,000), arm's-length contractor payments ($200,000), and restored ASA capital equipment ($300,000) yields $1,600,000 in total allowable SR&ED expenditures.
Part 5 Form T661 — Prescribed Proxy Amount (Line 820 / Line 502): Because the NRC IRAP grant does not reduce the Part 5 salary base, the PPA is 55% × $1,000,000 = $550,000.

Part 4 Form T661 — Pre-Assistance Federal Qualified Expenditures: Adding the $550,000 PPA to the $1,600,000 allowable expenditures and subtracting the 20% reduction (80% inclusion rule) on the $200,000 arm's-length contractor (−$40,000 on Line 529) yields $2,110,000 in gross qualified expenditures (composed of $1,810,000 in current expenditures plus PPA, and $300,000 in capital expenditures).
Deduction of NRC IRAP Grant: Subtracting the $250,000 NRC IRAP wage grant leaves $1,860,000 in post-IRAP qualified expenditures (composed of $1,560,000 net current plus PPA, and $300,000 capital).

Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Schedule 566 at 8%): Under section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the Ontario Ministry of Finance includes 100% of current expenditures and 100% of qualified capital expenditures made on or after December 16, 2024 (up to the $3,000,000 Ontario cap). Thus, the OITC is 8% × $1,860,000 = $148,800 (100% refundable cash).

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Schedule 508 at 3.5%): Under section 38 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario), the 3.5% non-refundable ORDTC applies to the Ontario eligible expenditure base reduced by the OITC: 3.5% × ($1,860,000 − $148,800) = 3.5% × $1,711,200 = $59,892 (non-refundable). If the CCPC is in a tax-loss position and prefers not to grind its 35% refundable federal ITC by a 3.5% non-refundable provincial credit, it may formally waive the ORDTC on Schedule 508 under subsection 43(1) of the Ontario Act by the filing-due date. Assuming the CCPC claims both OITC and ORDTC, total provincial government assistance entered on Line 513 of Form T661 is $148,800 + $59,892 = $208,692.

Net Federal Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570 of Form T661): Subtracting the $208,692 of Ontario tax credits from $1,860,000 leaves $1,651,308 in net federal qualified SR&ED expenditures (prorated as $1,384,968 in net current qualified expenditures and $266,340 in net capital qualified expenditures).

Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit (Schedule T2SCH31 at 35%): Because total net qualified expenditures ($1,651,308) are within the CCPC's $6,000,000 enhanced expenditure limit, the federal ITC on current expenditures is 35% × $1,384,968 = $484,739 (100% refundable = $484,739 cash), and the federal ITC on capital expenditures is 35% × $266,340 = $93,219 (40% refundable = $37,288 cash plus $55,931 non-refundable ITC). Total combined recovery across NRC IRAP ($250,000), OITC ($148,800), ORDTC ($59,892), and Federal SR&ED ITC ($577,958) equals $1,036,650 on $1,600,000 of cash R&D outlay (64.79% total recovery, including $920,827 in immediate cash).

body.text: 5.2 Deep Dive: Québec's New CRIC Regime (Post–March 25, 2025)

For taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Government of Québec replaced seven legacy tax incentives—the tax credit for salaries and wages of researchers, the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or research consortium, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for technological adaptation services, the industrial design component of the design tax credits, and the tax holiday for foreign researchers and experts—with the single Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC).

items: Elimination of Size-Based Rate Discrimination: Under the legacy Québec system, non-CCPCs or large corporations earned a base rate of 14% while only small CCPCs qualified for up to 30%. Under the CRIC, every eligible corporation with an establishment in Québec—whether a CCPC, a public corporation, or a foreign-owned subsidiary—receives a 100% refundable tax credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding $1,000,000 (shared among associated corporations via Form RD-1029.8.EN), with no corporate asset test.

Expansion to Pre-Commercialization and Capital Equipment: While the R&D component of CRIC remains harmonized with the federal subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED (and relies on the CRA for the scientific review of R&D work), CRIC newly covers pre-commercialization activities undertaken in Québec in conjunction with and as a continuation of R&D performed in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation. Eligible pre-commercialization activities encompass tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements and obtain initial approval or certification for commercializing an innovation, as well as product design (developing form and aesthetics, improving functionality, evaluating operational constraints, pilot-user validation, and selecting materials). Furthermore, CRIC includes 100% of property acquisition costs for new capital equipment used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec (excluding land, buildings, rights to use land or buildings, and property used in a large investment project holding an initial qualification certificate; cannot be combined with the C3i credit on the same expense), 100% of employee salaries, and 50% of amounts paid to a Québec subcontractor or eligible public research centre, research consortium, or university entity. Unlike federal SR&ED, CRIC does not provide a notional overhead proxy.

Modified Exclusion Threshold Calculation: Before applying the 30% and 20% credit rates on Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (filed alongside Form RD-222 for the Québec R&D deduction), a corporation's qualified expenditures must exceed an annual exclusion threshold corresponding to the greater of (1) $50,000, or (2) the sum across all eligible R&D and pre-commercialization employees of the basic personal amount (BPA) of the Québec personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025; $18,952 in 2026), adjusted for the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities. For example, a Québec team of 25 full-time employees in 2026 incurring $1,500,000 in eligible salaries faces an exclusion threshold of max($50,000, 25 × $18,952) = $473,800, leaving $1,500,000 − $473,800 = $1,026,200 in net qualified expenditures.

body.text: 6. Jurisprudence, Audit Precedents, and the "Why" and "How" Framework
6.1 Evolution from the Five Questions of Northwest Hydraulic to the CRA's "Why" and "How" Requirements

In Canadian tax jurisprudence, the foundational authority on what constitutes SR&ED is Justice Bowman's decision in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839 (T.C.C.), which was unanimously endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 (F.C.A.), CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88. Justice Bowman articulated five criteria (the Five Questions) to determine whether a project satisfies the statutory definition of SR&ED:

items: Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures? (If the resolution of the problem is reasonably predictable using techniques, procedures, and data generally accessible to competent professionals in the field, there is no technological uncertainty.)

Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty? (This involves a five-stage process: observation of the subject matter, identification of the problem, formulation of a hypothesis, testing of the hypothesis by experiment or analysis, and logical evaluation.)

Did the procedures adopted accord with established and objective principles of the scientific method, characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement and experiment, and the formulation, testing and modification of hypotheses?

Did the process result in a technological advancement, that is to say an advancement in the general understanding? (Note that most scientific research involves gradual, incremental progress rather than spectacular breakthroughs, and the rejection of a hypothesis is itself a technological advancement because it eliminates a possible solution.)
Did the taxpayer keep a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests and results as the work progressed?

body.text: In August 2021, the CRA replaced its archived 2012/2015 policy with simplified administrative guidelines (Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives) that present the five questions as two overarching requirements—the "Why" Requirement and the "How" Requirement—derived from subsection 248(1) and corresponding to Part 2, Section B of Form T661:

items: The "Why" Requirement (Scientific or Technological Advancement & Uncertainty — Questions 1 and 4; Form T661 Line 242 [350 words]): Why was the work conducted? The work must be conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving technological advancement by generating or discovering conceptual knowledge (such as theories or prediction models rather than routine factual data) needed to overcome a scientific or technological uncertainty arising from an insufficiency in the existing scientific or technological knowledge base (internal business resources plus reasonably available public sources). Success or failure in meeting project objectives is irrelevant to eligibility; however, circumventing an uncertainty via a workaround using available knowledge is ineligible. Characteristics indicating insufficient technological knowledge include situations where existing design methods are inapplicable, specifications do not conform to existing standards, there are too many variables or unknowns, parameters lie outside normal operating ranges, or system uncertainty arises from integrating components with interlocking constraints.

The "How" Requirement (Systematic Investigation or Search — Questions 2, 3, and 5; Form T661 Line 244 [700 words] & Line 246 [350 words]): How was the work carried out? Following standard business practices or trial-and-error troubleshooting is insufficient; the claimant must define the problem, advance a hypothesis consistent with known facts as a starting point, test the hypothesis by experiment or analysis, develop logical conclusions based on the results (Line 246), and keep contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.

cells: Meaning of "systematic investigation" and repeatability requirement.
Established that systematic investigation requires structured planning, hypothesis testing, and contemporaneous record-keeping sufficient to allow repeatability.
Statutory interpretation of SR&ED incentives and experimental production runs later sold.

Held that SR&ED legislation must be given a fair, liberal interpretation to encourage R&D in Canada, and allowed materials used in experimental runs that were later sold (prompting the enactment of ITC recapture rules in s. 127(27)).
Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839
Defining technological uncertainty, incremental advancements, and the 5-question test.
Articulated the Five Criteria; recognized "system uncertainties" (4 of 5 river/hydraulic engineering projects allowed); confirmed incremental progress and rejected hypotheses qualify.
RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087 & CW Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393
Appellate endorsement of the Northwest Hydraulic test and evidentiary burden.
Elevated Justice Bowman's five questions to binding appellate law across Canada and confirmed that objective documentary evidence of experimentation is required.
Alcatel Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2005 TCC 149
Whether employee stock options constitute an expenditure incurred on SR&ED.
Court allowed stock options as an SR&ED cost, prompting Parliament to amend the Act effective after Nov 14, 2005, to exclude stock option benefits from SR&ED salary or wages.
6379249 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 77 & Easyway Cattle Co. Ltd. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 211
Strict enforcement of the 18-month SR&ED filing deadline and prescribed forms.

Easyway Cattle confirmed that failing to file Schedule T2SCH31 containing prescribed information by the 18-month deadline is fatal to earning an ITC; 6379249 Canada accepted highly credible verbal evidence proving a project was filed.
Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 69
Distinguishing technological uncertainty from custom engineering and defining a hypothesis.
Clarified that a project must address a genuine technological uncertainty and that Question 2 requires formulating a testable hypothesis rather than custom engineering design.
Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88
Whether the "scientific method" is legally required when those words are absent from s. 248(1).
Unanimously rejected the taxpayer's argument, affirming that the scientific method (the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria) is legally required to establish SR&ED under s. 248(1).
CAE Inc. v. The King, 2022 FCA 178 (aff'g 2021 TCC 57; SCC leave dismissed 2023)
Whether non-forgivable government SADI loans with non-commercial terms are "government assistance".

Held that non-commercial public loans constitute government assistance under s. 127(9) and para. 37(1)(d)—which subsequently led Parliament to enact Bill C-69 (retroactive to Jan 1, 2020) carving out bona fide "excluded loans" under s. 12(11).
Taxpayer win: confirmed that overcoming systemic uncertainty in integrating open-source tools to resolve performance bottlenecks goes beyond routine debugging/optimization and qualifies as SR&ED.
Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC)
Food science shelf-stability; application of known preservatives in a novel context; documentation standards.

Taxpayer win: held that technological uncertainty can exist even where a publicly available solution exists if never used in the specific context, and clarified that contemporaneous records need only track hypotheses, tests, and measurable results.
Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 173
Plagiarized technical narratives, statute-barred reassessments, gross negligence penalties (s. 163(2)), and s. 160 shareholder liability.

Split outcome: allowed 2007–2008 projects supported by physical evidence and test results, but denied 2006 & 2009 claims and upheld statute-barred reassessments, s. 163(2) gross negligence penalties, and s. 160 shareholder assessments because technical reports copied supplier website text.
Willowglen Systems Inc. v. The King, 2026 TCC 7
Software/systems engineering: SIL 4 train-control box vs. SCADA system upgrade.

Split outcome: allowed the safety-critical SIL 4 train-control project (MTCLM) due to cumulative system uncertainty, but disallowed $1,293,692 on the SCADACOM-5 project because modernizing and scaling up software using known tools is product development.

body.text: 7. Governing Bodies, Filing Deadlines, Pre-Claim Approval, and Dispute Resolution
7.1 Statutory Filing Deadlines and Prescribed Forms (No Extensions Permitted)

Under subsection 37(11) and subsection 127(9) of the Act, a taxpayer must file the prescribed forms containing the prescribed information on or before the SR&ED reporting deadline, which is 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing-due date for the taxation year in which the expenditure was incurred:

items: Corporations (T2 Return): Because a corporation's T2 filing-due date is 6 months after the end of its taxation year, the corporate SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after the end of the taxation year (for example, a taxation year ending December 31, 2025, has a T2 due date of June 30, 2026, and an absolute SR&ED reporting deadline of June 30, 2027). Both Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) must be filed on or before this 18-month deadline.

Individuals / Sole Proprietorships (T1 Return): Because an individual's T1 filing-due date is June 15 of the following calendar year, the SR&ED reporting deadline for Form T661 and Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals)) is June 15 of the second following year (17.5 months after the December 31 year-end).
Trusts (T3 Return): 90 days after the trust's tax year-end plus 12 months.

Partnerships (T5013 Return): Because a partnership cannot carry forward a Section 37 pool balance (it must deduct the full pool in computing partnership net income in the year under paragraph 96(1)(e.1)) and allocates ITCs to partners under subsection 127(8), the partnership's Form T661 should be filed with its T5013 Partnership Information Return no later than the earliest partner's SR&ED reporting deadline, and each partner must file its respective Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) by its own reporting deadline (if exempt from filing T5013 forms, each partner must attach a copy of the partnership's Form T661, financial statements, and ITC allocation schedule by their own reporting deadline).

body.text: Under subsection 220(2.2) of the Act, the CRA cannot by law extend the time or exercise ministerial discretion to accept prescribed information filed past the SR&ED reporting deadline. Claims using estimates, partially complete forms, or expressing an "intent to file" do not satisfy the filing requirements. If Form T661 is filed on time by the reporting deadline, but Schedule T2SCH31 (or Form T2038(IND)) is filed after the reporting deadline, the claimant may deduct the allowable SR&ED expenditures in the Section 37 pool, but is not entitled to earn any Section 127 ITC on those expenditures. The CRA recommends filing at least 90 days prior to the 18-month reporting deadline so that any missing prescribed information can be supplied before the deadline expires.
Mandatory Updates to Form T661 (May 15, 2026 Revision)

In the revised Form T661 updated on May 15, 2026 (alongside updated Forms T1145 and T1146 on May 15, 2026, Schedule T2SCH31 on May 22, 2026, and Schedule T2SCH49 on May 29, 2026), claimants must comply with the following prescribed reporting fields:

items: Line 207 (CRDC Field of Research Code): Enter the first five digits (RDF#####) of the Field of Research (FOR) code from Statistics Canada's Canadian Research and Development Classification (CRDC) 2020 Version 2.0.
Lines 212 & 214 (Pre-Claim Approval Case Number): Check Line 212 if optional Pre-Claim Approval was obtained, and enter the CRA case number on Line 214.

Part 2 Section B Project Descriptions (Top 20 Projects Rule): Claimants may submit Part 2 project details for only their 20 largest projects by dollar value, though complete project descriptions must be prepared and kept for every project claimed. The strict word limits are 350 words for Line 242 (scientific or technological uncertainties), 700 words for Line 244 (work performed in the tax year), and 350 words for Line 246 (advancements achieved).

Lines 262–263 & Part 6B / 6C (Restored Capital & SUE): On Line 262, enter the names of the 10 most expensive depreciable SR&ED properties per project acquired after December 15, 2024 (claimed on Line 390), and on Line 263 enter their percentage of SR&ED operating time; in Part 6B (Box 780) and Part 6C (Box 788), list the 20 most expensive depreciable capital properties and Shared-Use-Equipment items across all projects.

body.text: 7.2 Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026)

On April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the Optional Pre-Claim Approval process via My Business Account. Available to businesses with gross business income below $25 million, this optional service allows a taxpayer to submit proposed projects before SR&ED work begins or costs are incurred and receive a formal CRA determination within 8 weeks on whether the planned work meets the definition of SR&ED. Pre-Claim Approval evaluates project eligibility rather than expenditure amounts, and claimants must still submit Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 after year-end.
7.3 Claim Preparer Penalties (Subsection 162(5.1)) and Gross Negligence Penalties (Subsection 163(2))

items: Part 9 Claim Preparer Disclosure and the $1,000 Penalty (Subsections 162(5.1) to 162(5.3)): Part 9 of Form T661 requires mandatory disclosure of claim preparer information and billing arrangements (such as contingency fees, hourly rates, or flat fees). If required claim preparer information in Part 9 is missing, incomplete, or inaccurate, subsection 162(5.1) imposes a $1,000 penalty per claim, for which the claimant and the claim preparer are jointly and severally, or solidarily, liable (subject to a due-diligence exception under subsection 162(5.2)). Unlike expenditure claims, Part 9 is not subject to the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline.

Gross Negligence Penalties on Overstated Claims (Subsection 163(2)): Under the CRA's updated Gross Negligence Penalty on Overstated SR&ED Claims Policy (updated January 28, 2025, formerly Application Policy SR&ED 96-05) and subsection 163(2) of the Act, making or participating in a false statement or omission knowingly or under circumstances amounting to gross negligence triggers a penalty and permits the CRA to reassess statute-barred taxation years, as demonstrated in Les Éléments Chauffants Tempora Inc. v. The King (2025 TCC 173). Third-party advisors who counsel or participate in false claims are also subject to penalties under section 163.2.

body.text: 7.4 CRA Audit Procedures, Administrative Second Review, and Appeals

When an SR&ED claim is received, the CRA risk-assesses the submission and either accepts it as filed (with a target of 60 days for non-reviewed refundable claims) or selects it for a financial review, a technical review, or a coordinated review conducted by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA) and a Financial Reviewer (FR), guided by The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants (updated July 2, 2025). Processing targets for reviewed claims are 120 to 180 days for refundable claims and 365 days for non-refundable claims. Claimants must retain all supporting technical and financial books and records for a minimum of 6 years from the end of the last taxation year to which they relate.
If a dispute arises during a review, the claimant must navigate a four-stage resolution and appeal process:

items: Response to the RTA / FR Proposal Letter (30-Day Window): Prior to issuing an unfavourable decision (which requires consulting the Research and Technology Manager [RTM] if made without an on-site visit, if disallowing for lack of information, or if penalties/fraud are considered), the RTA/FR issues a Proposal Letter outlining the reasons for proposed disallowance. The claimant generally has 30 days to submit additional supporting evidence and engage directly with the RTA/FR and the RTM or Financial Review Manager (FRM).

Administrative Second Review (Form RC532): If issues remain unresolved with the RTM/FRM before the reassessment is finalized, the claimant may submit Form RC532 to the National Intake Centre to request an Administrative Second Review (ASR). Conducted by the regional SR&ED Assistant Director, the ASR evaluates whether the reviewers adhered to CRA policies and accorded the claimant procedural fairness.

Formal Notice of Objection (Strict 90-Day Statutory Deadline): Once a Notice of Assessment or Notice of Reassessment is issued (within the normal reassessment period of 3 years for CCPCs and 4 years for non-CCPCs), the claimant has 90 days from the date of sending of the Notice (or up to 1 year from the filing-due date for sole proprietors) to file a formal Notice of Objection online via My Business Account / Represent a Client or on paper Form T400A (with a one-year extension application window available only under strict extenuating circumstances). The file is assigned to an independent CRA Appeals Officer in the Appeals Branch, who issues either a Notice of Reassessment or a Notice of Confirmation (typically taking 12 to 24 months).

Appeal to the Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal: Following a Notice of Confirmation from the CRA Appeals Branch, the claimant may file a Notice of Appeal with the Tax Court of Canada (under either the Informal Procedure or the General Procedure), with a further right of appeal to the Federal Court of Appeal.
